Chapter 37

Live screens, and the stale phase

The bug where a refresh returned the old answer — and why the fix was to stop refreshing.

By the end of this chapter

Understand when refresh() is enough and when only a live query will do.

The venue console has a button that opens an instrument for trading. An operator presses it, and the phase badge on screen should change from auction to continuous.

It did not. It stayed on auction until you reloaded the page.

The code that looked right

That is the pattern from Part 4, and it is correct everywhere else in this app. Here it produced a screen that showed the wrong thing while reporting success.

Why it could not work

Look at what submit actually does. It appends a command to the log and returns the sequence number. That is all. The command has not been applied yet — the engine is a separate process, and it will pick the command up on its next poll, run it through the matching engine, and append the resulting phase_changed event.

So refresh() fires immediately, the query re-reads the projections, and the projections faithfully report the phase as it was — because it still is. The refresh worked perfectly. It was asking a question whose answer had not changed yet.

The gap is the architecture, not a bug in it

Every command in this system is asynchronous by design. That is what buys deterministic replay, a single ordering, and a venue that can be rebuilt from its log. The cost is that "I sent it" and "it happened" are two different moments, and any UI that conflates them will eventually show somebody a lie. You cannot patch this with a setTimeout — you have to build the screen around it.

The fix: stop asking, start listening

The command no longer refreshes anything. It appends and returns. The badge changes when the engine says so, which may be forty milliseconds later or, if the engine is down, not at all — and "not at all" is information the operator badly needs.

When refresh is enough

The rule that came out of this:

  • refresh() when the command's effect is complete by the time it returns. Creating an API key, adding a webhook endpoint, setting a feature flag — these write directly to a table, so the next read sees them.
  • query.live when the command goes through the log. Placing an order, cancelling, changing a phase, hitting the kill switch — the effect arrives later, from another process.

The test is not "does this change often?" — it is "who writes the value I am about to read, and have they finished?"

Note that the order blotter *does* still call refresh() after placing an order — but as best-effort immediacy, not as the truth. The gateway writes no rows: the blotter's working row appears in order_record only when the projector applies the engine's order_accepted event, so a refresh fired in the same response can only return the list as it stood before the engine ran. The REST API states the same gap out loud — its 202 body carries status: 'accepted' and tells the caller to watch the event stream for the outcome. The refresh is a cheap chance to be early; the event-driven data is what is guaranteed to be right.

The test that could never pass

One more trap, from driving this page in a browser:

networkidle waits for 500ms with no network activity. A page with a query.live connection has an open, deliberately long-lived request for as long as the page exists. The condition is never satisfied, and the failure is a timeout with no explanation.

Wait for the thing you actually care about instead — a selector, a row count, a piece of text. Which is better practice anyway: networkidle is a proxy for "the page is ready", and proxies are exactly what break when the architecture changes underneath them.

Checkpoint

  • You can explain why refresh() returned a stale phase without failing
  • You can state the rule for choosing between refresh() and query.live
  • You can explain why the blotter's refresh is correct and the console's was not
  • You know why networkidle never fires on a page with a live query
